bit_cast although safer isn't really a replacement in this case.  We should look at something that doesn't require a cast at all.  Something like pldm uses.  This patch itself is fine, but can you look into doing something that doesn't require a cast at all?
One way to avoid a cast is to use memcpy, but I remember we have discussed it and decided to not use it since it has performance overhead. To my knowledge, there are no more options other than that.

@ed@tanous.net, I have checked that libpldm uses its own msgbuf api which uses memcpy under the hood. So for this application, which approach do you suggest to replace the use of reinterpret_cast, using std::bit_cast or memcpy?

> One way to avoid a cast is to use memcpy, but I remember we have discussed it and decided to not use it since it has performance overhead

Can you be more specific about the `memcpy()` overhead concern? And do you have a performance target to measure against?

Hand-waving performance in the face of the sharp edges such as alignment, undefined behaviour, and resulting API ergonomics, not to mention that you're copying data for the purpose of endian-conversions anyway, means that there are some genuine trade-offs to consider here.

One particular sharp edge is you can't take a pointer to an object that isn't guaranteed to be aligned for its type (for instance when using `__attribute__((packed))`), which can make for a poor user experience. Specifying types to be amenable to casting over byte buffers (`__attribute__((packed))` again) can give the impression that one doesn't also need to handle endianness (that merely casting the buffer to the type and accessing the data is fine), not to mention that you're pushing that endian-handling responsibility onto all users of the type.

Further, it's often possible to come up with much nicer in-memory representations of data than the wire format, and explicit unpacking/packing between the two allows you to handle that ergonomically.

Returning to the `memcpy()` peformance concerns though, this is something that libpldm's msgbuf API design does account for (along with the points above). Taking, for example, the [`decode_pldm_platform_file_descriptor_pdr()` implementation](https://github.com/openbmc/libpldm/blob/main/src/dsp/platform.c#L3476-L3540) - while the msgbuf APIs appear to be quite verbose in their implementation (e.g. [pldm__msgbuf_extract_uint16()](https://github.com/openbmc/libpldm/blob/main/src/msgbuf/core.h#L528-L565)), inspecting e.g. the release-mode ARM disassembly shows [this all optimises to straight-line load/store pairs](https://gist.github.com/amboar/c1f06616e2a3c12846158f425d0168f2), with some conditional accesses towards the end to account for message-driven conditional data and variable-length portions of the message. This is also all protected against invalid buffer accesses without explicit length tests on the part of the `decode_pldm_platform_file_descriptor_pdr()` implementation - the msgbuf API injects those for us, and the optimiser automatically cleans up what it can prove is unnecessary. Further, building for big-endian will automatically provide the necessary byte manipulations with no work required by the codec implementation or the user of the struct.

I guess I'm trying to argue the merits of libpldm's approach (but I'm also going to be a bit biased there).

The packed struct are not used for parameters of encode/decode functions. The packed struct are strictly used inside encode/decode functions to avoid copying the the data. The encode/decode functions strictly has individual message fields as their parameters uint32_t, uint8_t, std::vector<uint32_t> etc (either by value or by reference). So the caller of the functions will always receive the data that is endianess correct and safe to use. The packed structs are used to avoid copying the data and build in place. These are comment on an initial patch for this app - 
https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/dbus-sensors/+/79826/comment/9c30db0d_4103e05a/
https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/dbus-sensors/+/79826/comment/764de301_e4e805fb/

I will further investigate libpldm approach and if its approach seems feasible for this app, I will create a follow up patch that follows libpldm approach for encode/decode.

memcpy on its own isn't a concern so long as there's a well structured API for reading values from a buffer that enforces endianess, alignment, and undefined behavior.  Using memcpy to cast to a struct (like @andrew@codeconstruct.com.au notes) is a sharp edge.  Using memcpy to cast to a base value that doesn't have endian issues (or has those issues solved) is far different.

I agree, I would be surprised if there were any performance issues between cast and memcpy.

From my perspective, I would like to see something similar to the msgbuf implementation implemented here.  IPMI uses a similar structure for unpacking ipmi messages.

I have Replaced the use of reinterpret_cast with memcpy for copying
data to and from the buffer. Only the encode/decode functions for two
MCTP VDM commands are updated. The remaining MCTP VDM commands’ encode/decode functions will be updated in a follow-up commit after this one is merged.
Overall I think this is a huge improvement.  If you want to merge as-is, this is fine as is, but I think a couple minor improvements could simplify further.

Rather than maintaining a separate offset, you could do buffer.remove_prefix(sizeof(T))

And just maintain the buffer itself.  That would also change getCurrentBufferPointer() to just return data()

And remove a bunch of extra math.
Done. Used subspan function of std::span instead.

?  Isn't this going to return 1?

Taking sizeof(uint8_t) seems weird
Made it explicit.
I would've made these immediately return an error, but fine as is.

FWIW, libpldm's msgbuf APIs do both. I recommend that. For some operations, particularly extractions, it's important to know whether the operation succeeded immediately. For instance, extracting the count member for a subsequent array, where you then need to use that count value to correctly extract the array. If extracting the count fails then there's no point proceeding.

More abstractly, what's important is testing result for extraction of any value that you subsequently need to use for a correct parse of a message.

However, the ergonomics of deferred error testing are nice, so I recommend doing that where it doesn't impact correctness of the implementation.
Agreed, both makes a ton of sense.
Using both the approaches now.

You shouldn't be acting on the dataSize if the unpack failed.  I suspect unpack() also needs to return an error of some kind?  Or you need to unpack everything first, then check for errors, then do this operation.
